title: Wrong Blood in Tube, Positive Patient ID and Choosing an LIS
summary: Learn what a wrong-blood-in-tube error is and why paperwork cannot catch it, how bedside barcode identification, strict acceptance policies and a separate group check sample prevent or detect it, and how labs weigh a best-of-breed LIS against an integrated EHR module.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 12 Hits 7 (wrong blood in tube) and 11 (LIS selection) and Trap 4 (integrated EHR-LIS). WBIT definition, harms, detection and prevention checked against Ning 2016, Snyder 2012 (read via a page-fetch tool), Sandhu 2017 (read via a page-fetch tool), Obaidallah 2022, Aghili Pour 2026 and Bolton-Maggs 2013; LIS selection against Tuthill 2014 and Sergi 2022. Not taught as fact: the reviewer’s list of modules missing from Epic Beaker (HLA, blood bank, cytogenetics, flow, NGS), the “mini-RFP” and “temporally close” demos, and the claim that integrated suites squeeze out stand-alone vendors (see register flag rv-lis-integrated-module-gaps). Barcode symbology (Hits 5–6, Trap 2) is not taught: no open source on 1D vs 2D error correction could be read (the GS1 DataMatrix guideline returned 403).

objectives: Define wrong blood in tube and explain why label-to-request checks cannot detect it.
Describe bedside barcode positive identification, restrictive acceptance policies and the group check sample.
Compare a best-of-breed LIS with an integrated EHR laboratory module and state how labs evaluate them.

cues.text: A nurse draws blood from two patients in neighbouring beds, then labels both tubes later at the nursing station.
Patient B’s blood ends up under Patient A’s label. The label and the request form match perfectly, and Patient A has no blood group on file.
Would anyone in the laboratory notice?

props.title: Bedside draw
lines: Patients A and B, side by side

scenes.title: What wrong blood in tube means
scenes.altText: Definition card: specimen identification errors include (i) a label that does not match the request, (ii) an unlabelled specimen, and (iii) a mislabelled specimen, also called wrong blood in tube (WBIT): the label names patient A, matching A’s request, but the blood is patient B’s. Harm card: wrong results can lead to misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment, and WBIT can lead to an ABO-incompatible transfusion, which may cause death or major morbidity. Detection card: a WBIT is hard to detect, because it needs a historical group or a second sample to reveal it; ABO-identical WBITs stay silent. UK haemovigilance (SHOT) reports about 100 wrong blood samples caught for every one that results in a wrong component transfusion.

cues.text: Specimen identification errors come in three kinds: a label that does not match the request, an unlabelled tube, and the worst, wrong blood in tube. The label and request both name patient A, but the blood belongs to patient B.
Wrong results can lead to a wrong diagnosis and wrong treatment. In the blood bank, a wrong blood in tube error can lead to an ABO-incompatible transfusion, which can kill.
These errors are hard to catch, because the paperwork looks correct. Only a historical blood group or a second sample reveals them, and if both patients share a blood group, the error stays silent.
UK haemovigilance reports about one hundred wrong blood samples caught for every one that leads to a wrong transfusion.

props.title: Hard to detect
lines: Needs a historical or second group

scenes.title: Positive identification by barcode
scenes.altText: Workflow card (one hospital’s system, Ning 2016): the nurse scans their own badge, then the patient’s barcoded wristband, then the barcoded tube label at the bedside; a mismatch triggers an alarm; the scan time is recorded as the collection time. Policy card: restrictive specimen acceptance; no relabelling of mislabelled or unlabelled specimens except irretrievable ones (such as CSF or tissue), with the collector coming in person to identify and sign. Outcome token: serial interventions cut identification errors from 0.0511% to 0.0015% (a 97% relative reduction). Evidence card: a CDC Laboratory Medicine Best Practices meta-analysis rated the evidence for barcoding high and recommended barcoding of specimen labels and point-of-care tests as best practice in hospitals. Second-sample card: a group check drawn as an independent second sample can detect WBIT before ABO-incompatible transfusion (some standards require it when electronic identification is not used).

cues.text: The fix is to take memory out of identification. At the bedside, the collector scans their badge, the patient’s barcoded wristband, then the tube label. If they do not match, the system raises an alarm.
Pair it with a strict acceptance policy: mislabelled or unlabelled tubes are not relabelled, except irretrievable specimens such as spinal fluid, and then only by the collector in person.

In one ten-year hospital study, these steps cut identification errors from about five in ten thousand specimens to under two in a hundred thousand. A best-practices meta-analysis recommends barcoding as an evidence-based practice in hospitals.

For transfusion, some standards require a group check when electronic identification is not used: a second sample, drawn separately, whose blood group must match the first. A mismatch exposes the wrong blood in the tube.

scenes.title: Choosing the system that carries the barcode
scenes.altText: Comparison cards (Tuthill 2014, API Strategic Summit): best-of-breed (BoB) LIS = a stand-alone LIS with optimum functionality compared with competing systems; enterprise-wide solution (EWS) = an LIS integrated into the EHR vendor’s suite. An EWS is optimal only if its LIS functionality matches or exceeds BoB; single-vendor integration is not guaranteed to beat well-implemented local integration; gaps (such as a missing transfusion-management module) force extra purchases, raising total cost of ownership. Toolkit card: about 850 functionality statements, a set of scenarios to guide on-site vendor demonstrations, and a total-cost-of-ownership worksheet. Implementation token (Sergi 2022, Epic Beaker): find mismatches with laboratory workflow early, through demonstrations to end users; instrument interfacing used Data Innovations middleware. Hook answer card.

cues.text: Barcodes only work inside a laboratory information system. Labs choose between a stand-alone, best-of-breed system and a laboratory module built into the hospital’s electronic health record suite.

From the laboratory’s point of view, the integrated module is the better choice only if its laboratory functions match the best stand-alone systems. A missing function, such as transfusion management, must be bought separately, raising the total cost of ownership.
So labs compare systems against detailed function lists, and guide vendor demonstrations with prepared scenarios, so that workflow gaps show up early.

Back to the hook: no one would notice from the paperwork. A bedside wristband and tube scan would likely have blocked the mislabel, and a separate group check sample would catch it before transfusion, unless the two patients share a blood group.

props.title: Hook answer
lines: Scan likely blocks it · group check catches it if ABO differs

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “A careful label-to-request check catches WBIT” (✓ in WBIT the label and request match; detection needs a historical group or a second sample, and bedside electronic identification helps prevent it); “Relabel a mislabelled tube at the bench to save a redraw” (✓ restrictive acceptance: recollect; relabel only irretrievable specimens, by the collector in person); “An integrated EHR-LIS is automatically best of both worlds” (✓ only if its lab functionality matches best-of-breed; gaps add cost).

cues.text: Trap one: a careful check of label against request catches wrong blood in tube. No: in this error they match. Only a historical group or a second sample exposes it; a bedside scan helps prevent it.
Trap two: relabel a mislabelled tube at the bench to save a redraw. No: recollect. Only irretrievable specimens are relabelled, by the person who collected them.
Trap three: an integrated health record system gives the best of both worlds. No: only if its laboratory functions match the best stand-alone systems.

props.title: ✗ “Label vs request catches WBIT.”
lines: ✓ They match; needs historical or 2nd group

scenes.title: Scan, scan, second draw
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “SCAN the person, SCAN the tube, then a SECOND DRAW tells the truth; and test-drive any LIS on YOUR roads, not the dealer’s.” Tokens: scan wristband · scan tube · second draw · your scripts. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: scan the person, scan the tube, and a second draw tells the truth. And test-drive any laboratory system on your own roads, not the dealer’s.

Where it breaks: scanning fails if staff bypass it or print labels away from the patient; a second sample cannot expose an error between two patients with the same blood group; and group check rules differ between countries and hospitals.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Group check rules vary by country

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “WBIT: label and request match, blood is someone else’s → bedside barcode scan, no relabelling, separate group check sample”, “LIS choice: integrated EHR module only if it matches best-of-breed functions; test with your own scripted demos”.

cues.text: Wrong blood in tube hides behind matching paperwork, so prevent it with bedside barcode identification and catch it with an independent second sample, and choose a laboratory system by testing its functions against your own workflow rather than trusting integration.

props.label: WBIT → bedside scan · no relabelling · separate group check
LIS: integrated only if it matches best-of-breed · scripted demos

explanation.what: Plain language: sometimes the tube carries the right name but the wrong person’s blood. Because the label and the request agree, no paperwork check can see it; scanning the patient’s wristband and the tube at the bedside prevents it, and a second, separately drawn sample can expose it. The computer system that runs this must be chosen for real laboratory functions, not for convenience. Scientific terms: specimen identification error, mislabelled specimen, wrong blood in tube (WBIT), positive patient identification, barcoded wristband, restrictive specimen acceptance policy, group check (second blood group determination), ABO-incompatible transfusion, haemovigilance, best-of-breed (BoB) LIS, enterprise-wide solution (EWS), total cost of ownership (TCO), middleware.
explanation.why: WBIT can cause misdiagnosis and ABO-incompatible transfusion with death or major morbidity. Errors arise when tubes are labelled away from the patient and are over-represented in busy areas such as the emergency department; electronic identification removes reliance on memory and was associated with large reductions in identification errors.
explanation.measure: One hospital: identification errors fell from 0.0511% to 0.0015% of specimens after a restrictive acceptance policy and barcode positive identification (97% relative reduction). LMBP meta-analysis: barcoding favoured (pooled odds ratio 4.39), evidence high, recommended in hospitals. SHOT: about 100 wrong blood samples caught for every one leading to a wrong component transfusion. A large study (Kaufman et al, cited by Obaidallah) reported WBIT about 1 in 3046 with manual identification vs 1 in 14,606 with electronic identification.
explanation.differs: Label-request mismatch or unlabelled tube (visible at reception) vs WBIT (invisible on paper). Prevention (bedside scanning) vs detection (historical group, independent group check sample). Best-of-breed stand-alone LIS vs LIS module in the EHR suite.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: identify WBIT from a scenario, choose the best prevention (bedside electronic identification) or detection (second sample), reject bench relabelling, and recognise that an integrated LIS must be judged on laboratory functionality.

comparisons.title: Preventing vs detecting WBIT

left.label: Prevent
points: Scan wristband and tube at the bedside
Label at the patient, never later

comparisons.distinguisher: Stop the mislabel at collection vs expose it before transfusion.

comparisons.title: Best-of-breed vs integrated LIS
comparisons.distinguisher: Laboratory functionality measured against your workflow.

mnemonic.text: SCAN the person, SCAN the tube, then a SECOND DRAW tells the truth; and test-drive any LIS on YOUR roads, not the dealer’s.
mnemonic.explanation: Bedside scanning prevents WBIT, an independent second sample detects it, and scripted demonstrations reveal LIS gaps.
mnemonic.limitation: Scanning fails when bypassed or when labels are printed away from the patient; a second sample cannot expose a mix-up between two patients with the same blood group; group check rules differ between countries and hospitals.

analogyLimitations: Workflow cards are schematic and describe one published hospital system.
Error-rate figures come from single studies and settings; rates vary widely between institutions.
takeaway: Wrong blood in tube hides behind matching paperwork, so prevent it with bedside barcode identification and catch it with an independent second sample, and choose a laboratory system by testing its functions against your own workflow rather than trusting integration.

questions.stem: A tube arrives labelled with Patient A’s name and number, matching Patient A’s request, but it contains Patient B’s blood. Which statement is correct?

options.text: This is wrong blood in tube; it cannot be found by comparing label and request
options.rationale: Correct. In WBIT the label and request agree; only a historical blood group or a second sample can expose it, and bedside electronic identification helps prevent it.

options.text: Reception staff will catch it by checking the label against the request
options.rationale: Incorrect. The label and request match, so this check passes.

options.text: It is an unlabelled specimen and should be relabelled
options.rationale: Incorrect. The tube is labelled, just with the wrong patient’s identity for its contents.

options.text: It is harmless if the two patients share a blood group
options.rationale: Incorrect. Same-group errors are silent, not harmless: the results still belong to the wrong patient and can mislead diagnosis and treatment.

questions.stem: A ward sends a mislabelled EDTA tube for a CBC. Under a restrictive specimen acceptance policy, what should the laboratory do?

options.text: Reject it and request a new, correctly labelled specimen
options.rationale: Correct. Under the published policy, relabelling is allowed only for irretrievable specimens; a CBC tube can be recollected.

options.text: Correct the label at the bench from the request form
options.rationale: Incorrect. Bench relabelling cannot confirm whose blood is in the tube.

options.text: Run it and add a comment to the report
options.rationale: Incorrect. A comment does not make a misidentified result safe to use.

options.text: Phone the ward and relabel it on verbal confirmation
options.rationale: Incorrect. In the published policy, relabelling is limited to irretrievable specimens and requires the collector in person.

questions.stem: Hospital executives propose replacing the laboratory’s stand-alone LIS with the LIS module of their EHR suite. According to the pathology informatics authors of the LIS functionality assessment toolkit, when is the integrated option optimal from the laboratory’s perspective?

options.text: When its laboratory functionality performs at or beyond the level of best-of-breed systems
options.rationale: Correct. Integration alone does not justify lost laboratory functions.

options.text: Always, because one vendor guarantees better integration
options.rationale: Incorrect. Single-vendor integration is not guaranteed to exceed well-implemented local integration.

options.text: When it has the lowest licence fee
options.rationale: Incorrect. Missing functions require extra purchases, hardware and staff, so total cost of ownership matters.

options.text: When the vendor’s own demonstration looks smooth
options.rationale: Incorrect. Demonstrations should be guided by prepared scenarios and shown to laboratory end users so that workflow gaps appear early.

PLoS One. 2016;11(8):e0160821. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0160821
references.usedFor: Three categories of identification error including WBIT definition; restrictive acceptance policy (no relabelling except irretrievable specimens, collector in person); bedside badge-wristband-tube barcode scanning with mismatch alarm; error rates 0.0511% to 0.0015% (97% relative reduction); in 2005 the emergency department supplied 20% of specimens but 41% of identification errors.

references.citation: Snyder SR, Favoretto AM, Derzon JH, et al. Effectiveness of barcoding for reducing patient specimen and laboratory testing identification errors: a Laboratory Medicine Best Practices systematic review and meta-analysis. Clin Biochem. 2012;45(13-14):988-998. doi:10.1016/j.clinbiochem.2012.06.019
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool (first part of the article). Barcoding for specimen labelling and POCT recommended as best practice in hospitals; pooled odds ratio 4.39; evidence rated high; mislabelled specimens sometimes called wrong blood in tube.

references.citation: Sandhu P, Bandyopadhyay K, Ernst DJ, et al. Effectiveness of Laboratory Practices to Reducing Patient Misidentification Due to Specimen Labeling Errors at the Time of Specimen Collection in Healthcare Settings: LMBP™ Systematic Review. J Appl Lab Med. 2017;2(2):244-258. doi:10.1373/jalm.2017.023762
references.usedFor: Read via a page-fetch tool. Definition of mislabelled specimen as WBIT; standardised labelling policies and laboratory-clinical collaboration recommended.

references.citation: Obaidallah N, Downie H, Colavecchia C, Callum J, Lin Y. Implementation of a blood bank generated tube for second blood group determination: Challenges, yield, and cost. Transfusion. 2022;62(4):784-790. doi:10.1111/trf.16838
references.usedFor: WBIT definition and consequences (misdiagnosis, ABO-incompatible transfusion); WBIT detection needs a historical or second sample; second blood group determination (required by CSA and AABB when electronic identification is not used, as reported there); higher WBIT rates in the emergency department; reported manual vs electronic identification WBIT rates (citing Kaufman et al.).

references.citation: Aghili Pour H, Fiedler SA, Hoch J, et al. Survey on Detected "Wrong Blood in Tube" Events Based on Data from German Blood Establishments: A Feasibility Study. Transfus Med Hemother. 2026. doi:10.1159/000552490
references.usedFor: ABO-identical WBITs as undetected “silent errors”; WBIT case definition.

references.citation: Bolton-Maggs PH, Cohen H. Serious Hazards of Transfusion (SHOT) haemovigilance and progress is improving transfusion safety. Br J Haematol. 2013;163(3):303-314. doi:10.1111/bjh.12547
references.usedFor: About 100 wrong blood samples caught per one resulting in wrong component transfusion; correct identification at sampling and bedside; example of two samples labelled away from the patients; ABO-incompatible transfusion as the most serious incorrect-component event.

references.citation: Tuthill JM, Friedman BA, Balis UJ, Splitz A. The laboratory information system functionality assessment tool: Ensuring optimal software support for your laboratory. J Pathol Inform. 2014;5(1):7. doi:10.4103/2153-3539.127819
references.usedFor: Best-of-breed vs enterprise-wide solution definitions; EWS optimal only if LIS functionality matches or exceeds BoB; single-vendor integration not guaranteed superior; missing functions (such as transfusion management) and total cost of ownership; toolkit with about 850 functionality statements and scenarios to guide on-site demonstrations; an EWS may suppress consideration of other LIS solutions.

references.citation: Sergi CM. Implementing Epic Beaker Laboratory Information System for Diagnostics in Anatomic Pathology. Risk Manag Healthc Policy. 2022;15:323-330. doi:10.2147/rmhp.s332109
references.usedFor: Finding workflow discrepancies early through demonstrations to end-operators in the laboratory; Data Innovations Instrument Manager middleware in a Beaker implementation; notes that one issue seen in the Clinical Pathology module seems to have been solved recently.

claims.text: Identification error categories; WBIT definition; label and request match.
WBIT consequences including ABO-incompatible transfusion; about 100 wrong blood samples caught per wrong transfusion (SHOT).
Detection requires a historical or second sample; ABO-identical WBITs are silent.
Bedside barcode positive identification; restrictive acceptance policy; error-rate reduction; LMBP barcoding recommendation.
Group check as an independent second sample; manual vs electronic identification WBIT rates.
claims.note: The manual vs electronic rates are cited by Obaidallah from Kaufman et al.; the primary study was not read.

claims.text: Best-of-breed vs integrated LIS; functionality and total cost of ownership; scripted demonstrations; middleware.

Reviewer’s list of modules missing from Epic Beaker (HLA, blood bank, cytogenetics, flow, NGS); “mini-RFP” with temporally close demos; integrated suites squeezing out stand-alone vendors; WBIT as the driver of every barcoding standard.
claims.note: Not taught as facts in this lesson. Tuthill 2014 says an enterprise-wide solution may suppress consideration of other LIS solutions, which partly supports the vendor-market claim, but it is still not taught.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer lists specific modules (HLA, blood bank, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, molecular/NGS) as missing from Epic Beaker. The open sources read support the general risk of functionality gaps in integrated LIS modules but do not verify this list, and vendor products change; the lesson teaches only the general principle.

The reviewer presents WBIT as the archetypal catastrophic event but does not say how it is detected. Open sources stress that WBIT needs a historical or second sample to detect and that ABO-identical errors stay silent; the lesson adds this context.

Group check (second sample) requirements and acceptance policies differ between countries and hospitals; the sources read are from Canada, Taiwan, the UK, Germany and US-funded reviews. Philippine requirements are not covered.

morphology.note: No images; workflow and systems shown as schematic cards.

verification.notes: 6 claims checked against eight open sources (two read via a page-fetch tool); 1 pending (reviewer’s Beaker module list, mini-RFP details, vendor-market and barcoding-standard claims). No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
